claims.text: Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Resistance to temper embrittlement enables the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Temperature variation is the intervention used to induce the transition.
The relevant behavior occurs within a narrow temperature window.
Alloy composition and microstructure mediate the response to temperature.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys resist temper embrittlement.
The predicted outcome is a ductile–brittle–ductile transition without a dramatic loss of ductility.
Conventional alloys exhibit temper embrittlement and provide the baseline comparison.
The relevant boundary is the temperature range in which conventional alloys undergo temper embrittlement.
The exact temperature range capable of producing the proposed behavior is unknown.
The specific alloy compositions capable of producing the proposed behavior are unknown.
Observation of a dramatic ductility loss in the candidate alloys within the same temperature window as conventional alloys would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Resistance to temper embrittlement is presented as the cause of a ductile–brittle–ductile transition, although suppressing embrittlement would ordinarily remove the proposed brittle stage rather than generate it.

A brittle intermediate state is predicted while the same outcome is described as occurring without a dramatic loss of ductility, leaving the defining mechanical signature of the brittle state internally unclear.
